passages.title: Job loses his children and wealth
passages.summary: Job lives in the land of Uz and is blameless and rich. He has seven sons and three daughters and offers sacrifices for them. In heaven the accuser, called Satan, comes before the LORD. The LORD praises Job, and Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing. The LORD lets him take all that Job has. In one day raiders, fire, and a great wind destroy his herds, servants, and children. Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships. He says the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads the heavenly exchange as poetry about an accuser’s challenge. What does verse 1 tell the reader about Job?

contextNote.title: The reader knows what the friends do not
contextNote.text: The book’s first verse gives a verdict before any trouble comes. Job is blameless and upright, fears God, and turns from evil. The LORD repeats those words in verse 8. Satan’s question in verse 9 sets the test: is such goodness only paid for? Job and his friends never hear this scene in heaven. The reader does. Every later claim that Job must have sinned is already known to be wrong.

passages.title: Illness and silent friends
passages.summary: Satan comes before the LORD again. He says a man will give anything to save his own skin. The LORD lets him strike Job’s body but spare his life. Job is covered with painful sores from head to foot. He sits in ashes and scrapes himself with broken pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that people must accept hardship from God as well as good. Three friends come to comfort him and sit with him in silence for a week.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear. What do the friends do for seven days (verse 13)?

contextNote.title: Silence comes before the argument
contextNote.text: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar agree together to come and comfort Job (verse 11). They do not recognize him at first. They weep, tear their robes, and throw dust on their heads (verse 12). Verse 13 says they sat on the ground with him for seven days. No one spoke, because they saw how great his grief was. This silence is the best thing they do in the book. The trouble between them starts when they begin to explain.

passages.title: Job wishes he had not been born
passages.summary: After seven days Job speaks. He curses the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He wants that day turned to darkness and left out of the calendar. He asks why he did not die at birth. In the grave, he says, the weary rest and the slave is free. He asks why life is given to people in misery. What he feared most has happened. He has no ease, no quiet, and no rest.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering. What does Job curse in verse 3?

contextNote.title: Grief reverses the language of birth
contextNote.text: Satan said Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). In verse 3 Job curses his birthday. He never curses God in this chapter. Verse 4 says, “Let that day be darkness.” That reverses the first words of creation in Genesis 1:3. His speech is made of “why” questions (verses 11, 12, 20). The text records his grief at full length and adds no rebuke.

passages.title: Eliphaz explains suffering through guilt
passages.summary: Eliphaz of Teman speaks first, and he begins gently. He says Job has taught and strengthened many people. Now trouble has reached Job, and he is shaken. Eliphaz asks who ever perished while innocent. In his experience those who sow trouble reap it. He tells of a night vision that made his bones shake. A voice asked whether a mortal can be more just than God. Even God’s servants in heaven are not beyond fault.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt. What does Eliphaz say has happened to Job in verse 5?

contextNote.title: Past counsel becomes a charge
contextNote.text: Eliphaz opens with praise for Job’s past help to others (verses 3–4). Verse 5 turns that praise into a charge. Job could counsel sufferers, and now he cannot bear his own trouble. Verse 7 states the rule behind every speech the friends will make. The innocent do not perish. Eliphaz supports it from experience and from a vision (verses 8, 12–16). The reader knows from 1:1 that the rule does not fit this case.

passages.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction
passages.summary: Eliphaz continues. He says resentment kills the fool, and trouble does not grow from the ground. People are born to trouble as sparks fly upward. In Job’s place he would take his case to God. God does great things, sends rain, and lifts up the lowly. The person God corrects is happy, so Job should not reject discipline. God wounds, and he also heals. Job will yet have safety, many children, and a long life.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job. What does Eliphaz call Job’s suffering in verse 17?

contextNote.title: Advice assumes an explanation
contextNote.text: Much of what Eliphaz says here is fine teaching. Proverbs 3:11–12 says nearly the same as verse 17. The fault lies in where he applies it. He assumes Job’s pain is correction for a wrong. Chapter 1:8 has told the reader otherwise. His promises in verses 19–26 depend on Job accepting that account. Verse 27 closes the matter: we have searched it out, and it is so.

passages.title: Job asks his friends for kindness
passages.summary: Job answers Eliphaz. He says his grief would outweigh the sand of the sea. The arrows of the Almighty are in him. He wishes God would crush him and end it. He says a despairing person should have kindness from a friend. His friends are like a stream that dries up in the heat. Caravans turn aside to it and find nothing. He asks them to show him plainly where he has gone wrong.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?

contextNote.title: Failed friendship becomes a dry stream
contextNote.text: Verse 14 says what Job wanted: kindness for a man who is failing. Verse 15 says what he got. He compares his friends to a desert stream. It runs full with melted ice in the cold season (verse 16). In the heat, when travelers need it, it is gone (verse 17). Caravans leave the road for it and die (verses 18–20). In verse 24 he asks them to name his error, which none has done.

passages.title: Job addresses God in his pain
passages.summary: Job says human life is like the hard service of a hired worker. He has months of emptiness and nights of misery. His skin is broken, and his days pass faster than a weaver’s shuttle. He turns and speaks to God directly. He asks whether he is a sea monster that needs a guard. God frightens him with dreams. He asks why God watches a human being so closely. He asks why God does not pardon him before he lies in the dust.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?

contextNote.title: Attention can feel like pursuit
contextNote.text: From verse 7 on Job speaks to God, not about him. The friends never address God in the whole book. Psalm 8:4 asks, “What is man, that you think of him?” There the question is wonder at God’s care. Job asks nearly the same in verse 17 and means the opposite. God’s attention feels like being watched every moment (verse 18). In verse 19 he asks for time enough to swallow.

passages.title: Bildad blames wrongdoing
passages.summary: Bildad of Shuah answers Job. He calls Job’s words a great wind. He asks whether God ever bends justice. If Job’s children sinned, God gave them what they earned. If Job will seek God and is pure, God will restore him. Bildad tells him to ask earlier generations. A reed without water withers, and so does the hope of the godless. God will not reject a blameless man and will yet fill Job’s mouth with laughter.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame. What does Bildad say about Job’s children in verse 4?

contextNote.title: An argument makes the dead guilty
contextNote.text: Bildad begins from a principle in verse 3: God does not pervert justice. Verse 4 applies it to ten dead children. He says “if,” but his meaning is plain. They died because they sinned. Chapter 1:5 showed Job offering sacrifices for them in case they had. Chapter 1:19 said a wind killed them. Bildad keeps his principle safe by making the dead guilty.

passages.title: Job asks who could judge his case
passages.summary: Job agrees that no one can be in the right against God. God moves mountains, shakes the earth, and made the stars. He passes by, and Job cannot see him. Even if Job were innocent, his own mouth would condemn him. He says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike. His days run past like a swift messenger. God is not a man whom he could meet in court. There is no umpire to lay a hand on them both.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?

contextNote.title: A court requires more than an argument
contextNote.text: Job does not dispute God’s power; that power is his problem. The chapter is full of court language: answer, contend, judge (verses 3, 14–16, 32). A fair hearing needs two parties who can face each other. Verse 32 says God is not a man as Job is. Verse 33 names what is missing: an umpire over both. Job says no such person exists. The idea returns and grows in 16:19 and 19:25.

passages.title: Job asks why his maker harms him
passages.summary: Job says he will speak freely in his bitterness. He asks God to show him why they are in dispute. He asks whether God enjoys crushing what his own hands made. God knows that Job is not guilty. Job recalls being shaped like clay and knit together with bones. God gave him life and watched over his spirit. Yet God seems to have kept this suffering in store. Job asks to be left alone before he goes to the land of darkness.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?

contextNote.title: Creation becomes grounds for complaint
contextNote.text: Verse 8 sets two acts of the same hands together: making and destroying. Verses 9–12 describe his forming with great tenderness. He was shaped like clay, clothed with skin, and given life and kindness. Psalm 139:13–15 uses such images for praise. Job uses them as grounds for complaint. A maker should not ruin his careful work (verse 3). The memory of care makes the present harder to understand.

passages.title: Zophar demands that Job change
passages.summary: Zophar of Naamah answers. He says such a flood of talk must not go unanswered. Job claims to be pure, and Zophar wishes God would speak against him. God, he says, is punishing Job less than he deserves. No one can measure the depths of God. If Job puts away sin, he will lift his face without shame. His trouble will pass like water gone by. The eyes of the wicked will fail.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing. What does Zophar say about what Job deserves (verse 6)?

contextNote.title: Certainty closes the hearing
contextNote.text: Zophar is the harshest of the three. Verse 6 says Job has received less than his guilt deserves. In verse 5 he claims to know what God would say. When God does speak in chapters 38–41, he says nothing of the kind. Chapter 42:7 says the friends did not speak rightly. Zophar himself declares that God’s depths cannot be searched (verses 7–9). That truth should have made him less certain.

passages.title: Job challenges his friends’ wisdom
passages.summary: Job answers with sarcasm that wisdom will die with his friends. He has understanding as well as they do. He has become a joke to his neighbors, though he is upright. Robbers live in peace. Even the animals know that the LORD’s hand has done this. Wisdom and strength belong to God. He tears down, and no one rebuilds. He makes counselors, judges, and kings foolish and leads nations astray.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends. What does Job say the animals know (verses 7–9)?

contextNote.title: Creation does not settle the dispute
contextNote.text: The friends speak as if they hold a secret about God. In verses 7–9 Job says the birds and fish know it too. God’s hand is behind all that happens. That fact is common ground. What it means is the dispute. Verse 6 offers Job’s evidence: robbers live safely. Verses 13–25 list God’s power as overturning rulers, with no clear pattern of reward.

passages.title: Job seeks a hearing with God
passages.summary: Job says he knows all that his friends know. He wants to argue his case with God himself. He calls his friends liars and useless doctors. Their silence would be their wisdom. He asks whether they will speak falsely on God’s behalf. He warns that God will rebuke them for it. He will keep to his ways before God, whatever it costs. He asks God to remove his hand and tell him his sins.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. How does that reading differ from the World English Bible here?

contextNote.title: Defending God can involve false speech
contextNote.text: Verse 4 calls the friends “forgers of lies.” Verses 7–8 explain the charge. They say untrue things about Job in order to defend God. Job asks whether God needs that kind of help. He predicts in verse 10 that God will rebuke them. Chapter 42:7 records that rebuke. Verse 5 says their silence would have been wisdom, as it was in 2:13.

passages.title: Job asks whether the dead live again
passages.summary: Job says human life is short and full of trouble. A person blooms like a flower and fades like a shadow. A cut tree may sprout again at the scent of water. A person lies down and does not rise. Job wishes God would hide him in the grave until the anger passes. He asks whether someone who dies will live again. He would wait for God to call and long for him. But water wears away stone, and God wears away human hope.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this question with resurrection through Jesus Christ. What does Job ask God to remember?

contextNote.title: A tree offers hope people lack
contextNote.text: Verses 7–9 describe a stump that grows again when water reaches it. Verse 10 sets a human death against that picture. Job sees more hope for a tree than for himself. Then in verses 13–15 he imagines an exception. God might hide him, set a time, and remember him. He pictures God longing for the work of his hands. It is a wish, and verses 18–19 let it erode again.

passages.title: Eliphaz condemns Job’s words
passages.summary: Eliphaz speaks a second time, and his tone is sharper. He says Job’s words are hot wind. Job’s talk undermines reverence for God. His own mouth condemns him. Eliphaz asks whether Job was the first man born or sat in God’s council. He asks why God’s comforts are too small for Job. No human is pure before God. The wicked man lives in pain and dread and loses all he has.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?

contextNote.title: A friend treats protest as danger
contextNote.text: In chapters 4–5 Eliphaz was courteous. Here he opens with scorn (verses 2–3). Verse 4 makes a new charge. Job’s protest, he says, damages reverence and prayer for everyone. Verse 6 treats the protest itself as evidence of guilt. A man who complains this way must have something to hide. The portrait of the wicked in verses 20–35 is drawn to resemble Job’s losses.

passages.title: Job calls his friends poor comforters
passages.summary: Job calls his friends miserable comforters. He could talk as they do if they were in his place. He would instead strengthen them with his words. He says God has worn him out and torn him in anger. God set him up as a target and broke him. His face is red with weeping, though his hands are clean. He cries to the earth not to cover his blood. Even now, he says, his witness is in heaven.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame. What does Job call his friends in verse 2?

contextNote.title: A witness is needed beyond the friends
contextNote.text: Verse 2 gives Job’s verdict on the friends. Verses 4–5 say what he would do in their place. He would use his mouth to strengthen and ease grief. He then describes God as an attacker (verses 9–14). Yet in verse 19 he says he has a witness in heaven. He appeals to God against what God has done to him. The friends have failed, so he looks for an advocate above them.

passages.title: Job sees his hope nearing the grave
passages.summary: Job says his spirit is broken and the grave is ready. Mockers surround him. He asks God to put up a pledge for him, since no one else will. He has become a byword among the people. He says the upright will be appalled at this. He finds no wise man among his friends. His plans are broken off. If the grave is his home, he asks, where is his hope?
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?

contextNote.title: False brightness cannot remove death
contextNote.text: The friends keep promising Job a bright future if he repents. Zophar said his darkness would become like morning (11:17). In verse 12 Job answers that promise. They call night day and say light is near while it is dark. He will not accept comfort that denies what he sees. Verses 13–16 state his honest expectation, which is the grave. A hope that ignores his condition is no help to him.

passages.title: Bildad describes the wicked person’s ruin
passages.summary: Bildad speaks again and is offended. He asks why Job treats his friends as stupid animals. He asks whether the earth should be rearranged for Job’s sake. The light of the wicked goes out. His own schemes throw him down, and traps wait on every side. Terrors chase him, and disease eats his skin. His tent is destroyed, and his name is forgotten. He leaves no child or descendant among his people.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?

contextNote.title: A general picture targets one sufferer
contextNote.text: Verses 8–10 use six different words for traps and snares. Bildad says the wicked man walks into them by his own feet. The speech is framed as a general truth. Its details are not general. Disease consumes the skin (verse 13), and the tent is ruined (verse 15). Verse 19 says he has no child left. Each item matches what happened to Job.

passages.title: Job asks for pity and a defender
passages.summary: Job asks how long his friends will crush him with words. He says God has wronged him and closed his path. God has stripped his honor and uprooted his hope. His relatives, guests, and servants treat him as a stranger. His wife and children turn from him. He begs his friends for pity. He wishes his words were cut in rock forever. He says he knows his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ. A redeemer saves or defends someone. What help does Job hope for?

contextNote.title: An appeal interrupts accusation
contextNote.text: Verses 13–19 list every bond Job has lost, from brothers to servants to wife. The three friends are all he has left. Verse 21 begs them twice for pity. Verse 22 says they pursue him as God does. Since they give none, he turns elsewhere. He wants a written record (verses 23–24) and a living Redeemer (verse 25). In Leviticus 25:25 a redeemer is a relative who steps in to help.

passages.title: Zophar says wicked success ends quickly
passages.summary: Zophar says Job’s insult forces him to reply. He says the joy of the wicked is short. A wicked man may rise to the sky, yet he vanishes like a dream. His children must repay the poor. Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to poison inside him. He swallows riches and vomits them up. He crushed the poor and seized houses he did not build. Heaven exposes his guilt, and God’s anger is his portion.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?

contextNote.title: Zophar pictures wealth as swallowed food
contextNote.text: Zophar builds his speech on pictures of eating (verses 12–23). Wickedness tastes sweet and then turns to venom. Verse 15 says God makes the man vomit up his wealth. The claim under the pictures is in verse 5. The success of the wicked is brief. Verse 19 adds a charge of crushing the poor, with no proof. This is Zophar’s last speech, and Job answers it with evidence in chapter 21.

passages.title: Job points to wicked people who prosper
passages.summary: Job asks his friends to listen, and that will be their comfort. He asks why the wicked live long and grow strong. Their children are settled, and their houses are safe. They sing and dance and die in peace. They tell God to leave them alone. Job asks how often their lamp really goes out. One person dies at ease and another in bitterness, and both lie in the dust. Travelers report that the evil man is spared and buried with honor.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering. What does Job ask in verse 7?

contextNote.title: Observation challenges the friends’ rule
contextNote.text: The friends argue from a rule. Job argues in this chapter from what people can see. Verse 7 puts his question plainly. Verse 8 answers Bildad’s claim that the wicked leave no children (18:19). Verse 13 answers Zophar’s claim that their joy is short (20:5). In verse 19 he rejects the idea that the children pay later. Psalm 73:3–12 and Jeremiah 12:1 raise the same question.

passages.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
passages.summary: Eliphaz speaks a third time. He asks whether God gains anything from a person’s goodness. He says Job’s wickedness must be great. He accuses Job of taking pledges from the poor and stripping them. He says Job refused water, bread, and help to widows and orphans. That is why traps and terror surround him. Job should make peace with God and return to him. Then God will hear his prayers and make his ways bright.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help. What does Eliphaz accuse Job of in verse 6?

contextNote.title: Suspicion becomes an invented charge
contextNote.text: Until now the friends have hinted at guilt. In verses 6–9 Eliphaz names crimes. He offers no witness and no instance. The charges are built to fit the theory that suffering proves sin. Chapter 1:8 gives God’s own opposite verdict. Job will answer each charge in 29:12–16 and 31:16–22. Verse 30 says a clean man’s prayer can rescue the guilty (see 42:8).

passages.title: Job searches for God’s court
passages.summary: Job says his complaint is still bitter. He wishes he knew where to find God. He would lay out his case and hear the answer. He believes God would listen and not overpower him. He looks east, west, north, and south and cannot see God. Yet God knows the way Job takes. When tested, he says, he will come out like gold. Still he is terrified, for God does whatever he chooses.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions. What does Job wish he knew in verse 3?

contextNote.title: Absence prevents a hearing
contextNote.text: Job wants a courtroom, and he is confident of a fair hearing (verses 6–7). His problem in verse 3 is that he cannot find the judge. Verses 8–9 search in four directions and find no one. Verse 10 turns the matter around. Job cannot see God, but God sees Job’s path. He expects the test to prove him gold. Verses 15–16 show that this trust and his fear exist together.

passages.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
passages.summary: Job asks why God does not keep set times for judgment. People move boundary stones and steal flocks. They take the orphan’s donkey and the widow’s ox. The poor go naked in the cold and cling to rocks for shelter. They carry sheaves and go hungry. They tread the winepress and are thirsty. The dying groan in the city, and God charges no one. Murderers, adulterers, and thieves work in the dark.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses other Church scripture to study suffering. Which examples show Job’s concern for people beyond himself?

contextNote.title: A complaint extends beyond one household
contextNote.text: Job’s complaint now reaches past his own house. Verses 2–11 describe the poor in close detail. Workers carry grain while hungry and press grapes while thirsty (verses 10–11). Verse 12 gathers it up: the wounded cry out from the city. Job says God does not treat this as wrong. Eliphaz has just accused Job of crushing such people (22:6–9). This chapter shows whose side Job takes.

passages.title: Bildad questions human purity
passages.summary: Bildad gives the last and shortest speech of the three friends. He says rule and awe belong to God. God makes peace in his high places. His armies cannot be counted, and his light rises on everyone. Bildad asks how a human can be right before God. Even the moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight. A human being, he says, is a maggot and a worm.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

contextNote.title: A short speech leaves the case unheard
contextNote.text: The friends’ third round is running out of things to say. Bildad has six verses, and Zophar will not speak at all. Verse 4 repeats what Eliphaz said twice (4:17; 15:14). Job himself granted the point long ago (9:2). It does not touch his question about injustice in chapter 24. Verse 6 calls a human being a worm. In 1:8 God spoke of Job with pride.

passages.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
passages.summary: Job answers Bildad with scorn. He asks how Bildad has helped the weak or advised the unwise. Then Job describes God’s power himself. The dead tremble, and the grave lies open before God. He hangs the earth on nothing. He wraps water in clouds and marks the edge of light and dark. By his power the sea is stilled. These are only the fringes of his ways, a faint whisper.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

contextNote.title: Shared beliefs do not guarantee useful help
contextNote.text: Verses 2–4 are sarcasm. Bildad’s speech was grand, and it helped no one. Job then praises God’s power better than Bildad did (verses 5–14). He shows that knowledge of God’s greatness is not what divides them. They all believe it. Verse 14 calls everything he has listed a whisper. Job claims to know less about God than his friends claim.

passages.title: Job holds to his innocence
passages.summary: Job swears an oath by the living God, who has denied him justice. As long as he breathes, he will not speak falsely. He will never say that his friends are right. He will hold to his integrity until he dies. He asks what hope the godless have when God cuts them off. He then describes the fate of the wicked. Their children fall, and their silver passes to others. A storm sweeps them away in the night.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

contextNote.title: Job refuses a purchased agreement
contextNote.text: The friends offer Job a way out: confess, and be restored. Verse 5 calls that a lie he will not tell. He swears by the same God he says has wronged him (verse 2). Verse 6 says he holds fast his righteousness. God used that very language about him in 2:3. His wife used it against him in 2:9. Verses 13–23 sound like the friends’ view, and readers explain that in different ways.

passages.title: Where can wisdom be found?
passages.summary: This chapter is a poem about wisdom. People mine silver, gold, iron, and copper from the earth. Miners hang on ropes in shafts far from where anyone lives. They find sapphires where no bird or lion has gone. Yet no one knows where wisdom is found. It cannot be bought with gold or jewels. The sea and the grave do not hold it. God alone knows its place, and he says the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

contextNote.title: Mining skill exposes another limit
contextNote.text: Verses 1–11 admire human skill. Miners reach places the falcon and the lion have never seen (verses 7–8). Verse 12 then asks the question that skill cannot answer. Wisdom is not in the deep, and no price buys it (verses 14–19). Verse 28 gives God’s word to humans. To fear the Lord is wisdom, and to turn from evil is understanding. Those are the words used of Job in 1:1.

passages.title: Job remembers respect and service
passages.summary: Job begins his last speech by remembering better days. God’s lamp shone over him, and his children were around him. When he went to the city gate, young men stepped aside and elders stood. Princes stopped talking. He rescued the poor and the orphan. He was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He searched out the case of the stranger. People waited for his words as for rain.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

contextNote.title: Memory defines the lost public role
contextNote.text: Verse 12 begins with “because.” Job’s honor at the gate had a cause. Verses 12–17 list it: the poor, the orphan, the dying, the widow. He was eyes, feet, and a father to people in need. Verse 16 says he looked into the cases of strangers. Eliphaz charged him with wronging these same groups (22:6–9). Job answers with his record, point by point.

passages.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
passages.summary: Now, Job says, younger men mock him. Their fathers were outcasts he would not have hired. He has become their song, and they spit at him. God has loosened his bowstring and humbled him. Pain gnaws his bones at night. He cries to God and gets no answer. He once wept for people in trouble, yet evil came when he hoped for good. His harp is tuned to mourning.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

contextNote.title: The remembered world has been reversed
contextNote.text: The word “now” opens three parts of this chapter (verses 1, 9, 16). Each sets the present against the honor of chapter 29. Verse 20 names the deepest loss. Job cries out, and God does not answer. He stands, and God only looks at him. Verse 25 recalls that he wept for others in their hard days. He gave what he does not receive.

passages.title: Job gives his final defense
passages.summary: Job makes his final defense as a series of oaths. If he has lied, lusted, or cheated, let him be punished. He did not reject the complaints of his servants. One God made both him and them in the womb. He shared his bread with orphans and clothed the poor. He did not trust in gold or worship the sun and moon. He did not rejoice at an enemy’s ruin. He signs his defense and asks the Almighty to answer.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him. What does Job ask for in verse 6?

contextNote.title: A measure becomes an image of justice
contextNote.text: Job asks for a fair weighing of his life in verse 6. An even balance is an honest scale. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. Verses 13–15 ground a servant’s rights in one Maker of both. His standard reaches inward, to the eyes and to gloating (verses 1 and 29). In verse 35 he signs and demands a reply. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.

passages.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
passages.summary: The three friends stop answering, since Job holds that he is right. A younger man named Elihu has been listening. He is angry with Job for justifying himself and not God. He is angry with the friends for condemning Job without an answer. He waited because they were older. Now he says understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from years. He is full of words like wine with no vent. He promises to flatter no one.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

contextNote.title: Age does not settle authority
contextNote.text: Verse 8 states Elihu’s claim to speak. Wisdom comes from the Almighty’s breath, so age does not decide it (verse 9). That is a fair point against the three older men. The chapter also says four times that he was angry (verses 2–5). Verses 18–20 describe a man bursting to talk. Neither Job nor God ever answers Elihu. Chapter 42:7 names the three friends and leaves him out.

passages.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
passages.summary: Elihu asks Job to listen and answer if he can. He is made of clay as Job is, so Job need not fear him. He quotes Job’s claim to be innocent and wronged. He says Job is not right, for God is greater than man. God speaks in dreams to turn people from pride. He also warns through pain on a sickbed. A messenger may plead for the sick person and find a ransom. God does this again and again to bring a soul back from the pit.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

contextNote.title: An equal listener claims to explain God
contextNote.text: Job wanted someone on his own level to hear him (9:32–33). In verse 6 Elihu offers himself as that equal. He adds an idea the three friends did not develop. Suffering may warn and teach; it is not only a penalty (verses 16–19). Verses 29–30 say God uses it to bring people back. That is a real advance in the debate. It still assumes Job needed correcting, which 1:8 denies.

passages.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
passages.summary: Elihu speaks to the wise men who are listening. He quotes Job as saying God has taken away his right. He says Job drinks scorn like water and keeps company with evildoers. God cannot do wrong and repays each person’s work. If God withdrew his breath, all flesh would die. He shows no favor to princes over the poor. He sees every step and needs no inquiry. Elihu concludes that Job adds rebellion to his sin.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

contextNote.title: A principle takes the place of a hearing
contextNote.text: Verse 10 states a principle that the whole Bible affirms. God does not do wickedness. Elihu then uses it as a verdict on Job. If God is just, the man who complains must be wrong. Verse 11 repeats the friends’ rule that God repays each one’s work. Verses 7–8 accuse Job of walking with the wicked and cite nothing. A true principle takes the place of a hearing.

passages.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
passages.summary: Elihu asks whether Job thinks he is more right than God. He tells Job to look at the sky, far above him. Human sin does not harm God, and human goodness gives him nothing. Such things affect only other people. The oppressed cry out under the strong. Yet no one asks for God their Maker, who gives songs in the night. God does not answer an empty cry. So Job, who says he cannot see God, must wait.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

contextNote.title: Unheard cries receive another explanation
contextNote.text: Elihu grants in verse 9 that the oppressed cry out. Job said the same in 24:12. Elihu then explains why no answer comes. They cry from pain and do not truly seek God (verse 10). Verse 12 blames their pride. So an unanswered prayer becomes the fault of the one who prays. Job has already said his own prayer is pure (16:17).

passages.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
passages.summary: Elihu says he has more to say on God’s behalf. God is mighty and despises no one. He does not keep the wicked alive, and he gives the afflicted their rights. When people are bound in suffering, he shows them their wrong. If they listen, they finish their days in good. If not, they die without knowledge. Elihu warns Job not to turn toward evil. He then praises God, who draws up water and sends rain and thunder.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

contextNote.title: Instruction and threat share one speech
contextNote.text: Verse 15 sums up Elihu’s best thought. God rescues the afflicted by means of their affliction. Pain can open a person’s ear. Verses 11–12 then attach the old bargain: obey and prosper, refuse and perish. Job obeyed, and he did not prosper. So the teaching and a threat share one speech. In verses 27–33 Elihu turns to the storm, which prepares for chapter 38.

passages.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
passages.summary: Elihu’s heart pounds at the thunder. He says God’s voice roars, and lightning reaches the ends of the earth. God tells the snow and the rain to fall. Animals take cover, and ice forms by God’s breath. Clouds turn wherever he guides them. Elihu tells Job to stand still and consider these works. He asks whether Job knows how clouds are balanced. He ends by saying the Almighty is beyond reach and does not oppress.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

contextNote.title: Weather prepares a change of voice
contextNote.text: Verse 14 asks Job to stop and look at God’s works. Elihu’s questions in verses 15–18 sound like the ones God will ask. Verse 13 allows a storm more than one purpose. It may come for correction, for the land, or for kindness. That is wider than the friends’ single rule. A real storm seems to be gathering as he speaks. In 38:1 the LORD answers from the whirlwind.

passages.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
passages.summary: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. He asks who darkens counsel with words without knowledge. He asks where Job was when the earth’s foundations were laid. The morning stars sang then, and the sons of God shouted for joy. He asks who shut in the sea and commanded the dawn. He asks about the gates of death and the storehouses of snow. He sends rain on deserts where no one lives. He asks who feeds the lion and the raven.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth. What does God ask Job about creation?

contextNote.title: Questions change the scale of the debate
contextNote.text: Job asked for a hearing and thought none would come (23:3; 30:20). In verse 1 the LORD comes and speaks to him. The answer does not explain Job’s suffering. It never mentions the accuser or any charge. Verse 4 begins a long series of questions about the making of the world. Verses 26–27 describe rain falling where no person lives. The world is not arranged around human use or human reward.

passages.title: The Lord describes wild animals
passages.summary: The LORD continues to question Job about wild animals. He asks whether Job knows when mountain goats give birth. He asks who set the wild donkey free to roam the salt land. The wild ox will not plow or stay in a barn. The ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground and laughs at horse and rider. The war horse charges into battle without fear. The hawk flies south, and the eagle nests on the high cliff.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view. Who set the wild donkey free (verse 5)?

contextNote.title: Wild creatures live beyond human service
contextNote.text: Every animal in this chapter lives outside human control. Verse 5 asks who set the wild donkey free. Verses 7–8 show it scorning the city and ranging the hills. The wild ox serves no farmer (verses 9–12). The ostrich lacks sense, and God made her so (verses 13–17). The friends described a tidy world. God shows one full of misfits.

passages.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
passages.summary: The LORD asks whether the one who argues with the Almighty will correct him. Job answers that he is small and will say no more. The LORD speaks again from the whirlwind. He asks whether Job will condemn him in order to be right. He asks whether Job has an arm like God’s. Let Job humble every proud person and crush the wicked. Then God will admit that Job can save himself. He points to Behemoth, a huge creature that he made.
passages.uncertainty: The point shows the Jordan, which the poem names. It does not show Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views. What does God ask Job in verse 8?

contextNote.title: Judgment includes the power to govern
contextNote.text: Verse 8 names the real issue between them. To be in the right, Job has put God in the wrong. The friends did the reverse and put Job in the wrong. Both sides assumed that one of the two must be condemned. Verses 10–14 hand Job the task of governing. Let him bring down every proud person in the world. Running justice turns out to be harder than demanding it.

passages.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
passages.summary: The LORD describes Leviathan, a creature of the deep. No one can catch him with a hook or make him a servant. No one will play with him like a bird or sell him in the market. Harpoons and spears are useless. His scales are like rows of sealed shields. Fire and smoke come from his mouth. Iron is like straw to him. He looks down on everything proud and is king over them.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

contextNote.title: A creature resists the language of ownership
contextNote.text: Verses 1–7 ask whether Job can hook, bind, bargain with, or sell this creature. Verse 8 warns him to try once and remember it. Verse 10 draws the point. If no one dares to rouse Leviathan, who can stand before its maker? Verse 11 adds that God owes nothing to anyone. That answers the accuser’s question about serving God for pay (1:9). It also answers the friends’ view of reward as wages.

passages.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
passages.summary: Job answers the LORD. He says God can do all things. He admits that he spoke of things too wonderful for him. He had heard of God, and now his eye sees him. The LORD tells Eliphaz that the three friends did not speak rightly, as Job did. They must bring offerings, and Job will pray for them. When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes. Job receives twice as much, ten more children, and a long life.
passages.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s renewed life with hope after loss. What must the friends do after God corrects them?

contextNote.title: The final judgment changes how the speeches should be read
contextNote.text: Verse 7 changes how every speech in the book should be read. God says the friends did not speak rightly about him. He says his servant Job did, and repeats it in verse 8. Job protested, and the friends defended God. The honest protest is judged truer than the false defense. The friends now need the prayer of the man they accused. Verse 10 ties Job’s restoration to that prayer.

events.title: Job loses his children and wealth
events.summary: Job lives in the land of Uz and is blameless and rich. He has seven sons and three daughters and offers sacrifices for them. In heaven the accuser, called Satan, comes before the LORD. The LORD praises Job, and Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing. The LORD lets him take all that Job has. In one day raiders, fire, and a great wind destroy his herds, servants, and children. Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships. He says the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away.
events.detail: The book’s first verse gives a verdict before any trouble comes. Job is blameless and upright, fears God, and turns from evil. The LORD repeats those words in verse 8. Satan’s question in verse 9 sets the test: is such goodness only paid for? Job and his friends never hear this scene in heaven. The reader does. Every later claim that Job must have sinned is already known to be wrong.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads the heavenly exchange as poetry about an accuser’s challenge. What does verse 1 tell the reader about Job?

events.title: Illness and silent friends
events.summary: Satan comes before the LORD again. He says a man will give anything to save his own skin. The LORD lets him strike Job’s body but spare his life. Job is covered with painful sores from head to foot. He sits in ashes and scrapes himself with broken pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that people must accept hardship from God as well as good. Three friends come to comfort him and sit with him in silence for a week.
events.detail: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar agree together to come and comfort Job (verse 11). They do not recognize him at first. They weep, tear their robes, and throw dust on their heads (verse 12). Verse 13 says they sat on the ground with him for seven days. No one spoke, because they saw how great his grief was. This silence is the best thing they do in the book. The trouble between them starts when they begin to explain.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear. What do the friends do for seven days (verse 13)?

events.title: Job wishes he had not been born
events.summary: After seven days Job speaks. He curses the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He wants that day turned to darkness and left out of the calendar. He asks why he did not die at birth. In the grave, he says, the weary rest and the slave is free. He asks why life is given to people in misery. What he feared most has happened. He has no ease, no quiet, and no rest.
events.detail: Satan said Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). In verse 3 Job curses his birthday. He never curses God in this chapter. Verse 4 says, “Let that day be darkness.” That reverses the first words of creation in Genesis 1:3. His speech is made of “why” questions (verses 11, 12, 20). The text records his grief at full length and adds no rebuke.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering. What does Job curse in verse 3?

events.title: Eliphaz explains suffering through guilt
events.summary: Eliphaz of Teman speaks first, and he begins gently. He says Job has taught and strengthened many people. Now trouble has reached Job, and he is shaken. Eliphaz asks who ever perished while innocent. In his experience those who sow trouble reap it. He tells of a night vision that made his bones shake. A voice asked whether a mortal can be more just than God. Even God’s servants in heaven are not beyond fault.
events.detail: Eliphaz opens with praise for Job’s past help to others (verses 3–4). Verse 5 turns that praise into a charge. Job could counsel sufferers, and now he cannot bear his own trouble. Verse 7 states the rule behind every speech the friends will make. The innocent do not perish. Eliphaz supports it from experience and from a vision (verses 8, 12–16). The reader knows from 1:1 that the rule does not fit this case.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt. What does Eliphaz say has happened to Job in verse 5?

events.title: Eliphaz urges Job to accept correction
events.summary: Eliphaz continues. He says resentment kills the fool, and trouble does not grow from the ground. People are born to trouble as sparks fly upward. In Job’s place he would take his case to God. God does great things, sends rain, and lifts up the lowly. The person God corrects is happy, so Job should not reject discipline. God wounds, and he also heals. Job will yet have safety, many children, and a long life.
events.detail: Much of what Eliphaz says here is fine teaching. Proverbs 3:11–12 says nearly the same as verse 17. The fault lies in where he applies it. He assumes Job’s pain is correction for a wrong. Chapter 1:8 has told the reader otherwise. His promises in verses 19–26 depend on Job accepting that account. Verse 27 closes the matter: we have searched it out, and it is so.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job. What does Eliphaz call Job’s suffering in verse 17?

events.title: Job asks his friends for kindness
events.summary: Job answers Eliphaz. He says his grief would outweigh the sand of the sea. The arrows of the Almighty are in him. He wishes God would crush him and end it. He says a despairing person should have kindness from a friend. His friends are like a stream that dries up in the heat. Caravans turn aside to it and find nothing. He asks them to show him plainly where he has gone wrong.
events.detail: Verse 14 says what Job wanted: kindness for a man who is failing. Verse 15 says what he got. He compares his friends to a desert stream. It runs full with melted ice in the cold season (verse 16). In the heat, when travelers need it, it is gone (verse 17). Caravans leave the road for it and die (verses 18–20). In verse 24 he asks them to name his error, which none has done.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?

events.title: Job addresses God in his pain
events.summary: Job says human life is like the hard service of a hired worker. He has months of emptiness and nights of misery. His skin is broken, and his days pass faster than a weaver’s shuttle. He turns and speaks to God directly. He asks whether he is a sea monster that needs a guard. God frightens him with dreams. He asks why God watches a human being so closely. He asks why God does not pardon him before he lies in the dust.
events.detail: From verse 7 on Job speaks to God, not about him. The friends never address God in the whole book. Psalm 8:4 asks, “What is man, that you think of him?” There the question is wonder at God’s care. Job asks nearly the same in verse 17 and means the opposite. God’s attention feels like being watched every moment (verse 18). In verse 19 he asks for time enough to swallow.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?

events.title: Bildad blames wrongdoing
events.summary: Bildad of Shuah answers Job. He calls Job’s words a great wind. He asks whether God ever bends justice. If Job’s children sinned, God gave them what they earned. If Job will seek God and is pure, God will restore him. Bildad tells him to ask earlier generations. A reed without water withers, and so does the hope of the godless. God will not reject a blameless man and will yet fill Job’s mouth with laughter.
events.detail: Bildad begins from a principle in verse 3: God does not pervert justice. Verse 4 applies it to ten dead children. He says “if,” but his meaning is plain. They died because they sinned. Chapter 1:5 showed Job offering sacrifices for them in case they had. Chapter 1:19 said a wind killed them. Bildad keeps his principle safe by making the dead guilty.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame. What does Bildad say about Job’s children in verse 4?

events.title: Job asks who could judge his case
events.summary: Job agrees that no one can be in the right against God. God moves mountains, shakes the earth, and made the stars. He passes by, and Job cannot see him. Even if Job were innocent, his own mouth would condemn him. He says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike. His days run past like a swift messenger. God is not a man whom he could meet in court. There is no umpire to lay a hand on them both.
events.detail: Job does not dispute God’s power; that power is his problem. The chapter is full of court language: answer, contend, judge (verses 3, 14–16, 32). A fair hearing needs two parties who can face each other. Verse 32 says God is not a man as Job is. Verse 33 names what is missing: an umpire over both. Job says no such person exists. The idea returns and grows in 16:19 and 19:25.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?

events.title: Job asks why his maker harms him
events.summary: Job says he will speak freely in his bitterness. He asks God to show him why they are in dispute. He asks whether God enjoys crushing what his own hands made. God knows that Job is not guilty. Job recalls being shaped like clay and knit together with bones. God gave him life and watched over his spirit. Yet God seems to have kept this suffering in store. Job asks to be left alone before he goes to the land of darkness.
events.detail: Verse 8 sets two acts of the same hands together: making and destroying. Verses 9–12 describe his forming with great tenderness. He was shaped like clay, clothed with skin, and given life and kindness. Psalm 139:13–15 uses such images for praise. Job uses them as grounds for complaint. A maker should not ruin his careful work (verse 3). The memory of care makes the present harder to understand.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?

events.title: Zophar demands that Job change
events.summary: Zophar of Naamah answers. He says such a flood of talk must not go unanswered. Job claims to be pure, and Zophar wishes God would speak against him. God, he says, is punishing Job less than he deserves. No one can measure the depths of God. If Job puts away sin, he will lift his face without shame. His trouble will pass like water gone by. The eyes of the wicked will fail.
events.detail: Zophar is the harshest of the three. Verse 6 says Job has received less than his guilt deserves. In verse 5 he claims to know what God would say. When God does speak in chapters 38–41, he says nothing of the kind. Chapter 42:7 says the friends did not speak rightly. Zophar himself declares that God’s depths cannot be searched (verses 7–9). That truth should have made him less certain.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing. What does Zophar say about what Job deserves (verse 6)?

events.title: Job challenges his friends’ wisdom
events.summary: Job answers with sarcasm that wisdom will die with his friends. He has understanding as well as they do. He has become a joke to his neighbors, though he is upright. Robbers live in peace. Even the animals know that the LORD’s hand has done this. Wisdom and strength belong to God. He tears down, and no one rebuilds. He makes counselors, judges, and kings foolish and leads nations astray.
events.detail: The friends speak as if they hold a secret about God. In verses 7–9 Job says the birds and fish know it too. God’s hand is behind all that happens. That fact is common ground. What it means is the dispute. Verse 6 offers Job’s evidence: robbers live safely. Verses 13–25 list God’s power as overturning rulers, with no clear pattern of reward.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends. What does Job say the animals know (verses 7–9)?

events.title: Job seeks a hearing with God
events.summary: Job says he knows all that his friends know. He wants to argue his case with God himself. He calls his friends liars and useless doctors. Their silence would be their wisdom. He asks whether they will speak falsely on God’s behalf. He warns that God will rebuke them for it. He will keep to his ways before God, whatever it costs. He asks God to remove his hand and tell him his sins.
events.detail: Verse 4 calls the friends “forgers of lies.” Verses 7–8 explain the charge. They say untrue things about Job in order to defend God. Job asks whether God needs that kind of help. He predicts in verse 10 that God will rebuke them. Chapter 42:7 records that rebuke. Verse 5 says their silence would have been wisdom, as it was in 2:13.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. How does that reading differ from the World English Bible here?

events.title: Job asks whether the dead live again
events.summary: Job says human life is short and full of trouble. A person blooms like a flower and fades like a shadow. A cut tree may sprout again at the scent of water. A person lies down and does not rise. Job wishes God would hide him in the grave until the anger passes. He asks whether someone who dies will live again. He would wait for God to call and long for him. But water wears away stone, and God wears away human hope.
events.detail: Verses 7–9 describe a stump that grows again when water reaches it. Verse 10 sets a human death against that picture. Job sees more hope for a tree than for himself. Then in verses 13–15 he imagines an exception. God might hide him, set a time, and remember him. He pictures God longing for the work of his hands. It is a wish, and verses 18–19 let it erode again.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects this question with resurrection through Jesus Christ. What does Job ask God to remember?

events.title: Eliphaz condemns Job’s words
events.summary: Eliphaz speaks a second time, and his tone is sharper. He says Job’s words are hot wind. Job’s talk undermines reverence for God. His own mouth condemns him. Eliphaz asks whether Job was the first man born or sat in God’s council. He asks why God’s comforts are too small for Job. No human is pure before God. The wicked man lives in pain and dread and loses all he has.
events.detail: In chapters 4–5 Eliphaz was courteous. Here he opens with scorn (verses 2–3). Verse 4 makes a new charge. Job’s protest, he says, damages reverence and prayer for everyone. Verse 6 treats the protest itself as evidence of guilt. A man who complains this way must have something to hide. The portrait of the wicked in verses 20–35 is drawn to resemble Job’s losses.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?

events.title: Job calls his friends poor comforters
events.summary: Job calls his friends miserable comforters. He could talk as they do if they were in his place. He would instead strengthen them with his words. He says God has worn him out and torn him in anger. God set him up as a target and broke him. His face is red with weeping, though his hands are clean. He cries to the earth not to cover his blood. Even now, he says, his witness is in heaven.
events.detail: Verse 2 gives Job’s verdict on the friends. Verses 4–5 say what he would do in their place. He would use his mouth to strengthen and ease grief. He then describes God as an attacker (verses 9–14). Yet in verse 19 he says he has a witness in heaven. He appeals to God against what God has done to him. The friends have failed, so he looks for an advocate above them.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame. What does Job call his friends in verse 2?

events.title: Job sees his hope nearing the grave
events.summary: Job says his spirit is broken and the grave is ready. Mockers surround him. He asks God to put up a pledge for him, since no one else will. He has become a byword among the people. He says the upright will be appalled at this. He finds no wise man among his friends. His plans are broken off. If the grave is his home, he asks, where is his hope?
events.detail: The friends keep promising Job a bright future if he repents. Zophar said his darkness would become like morning (11:17). In verse 12 Job answers that promise. They call night day and say light is near while it is dark. He will not accept comfort that denies what he sees. Verses 13–16 state his honest expectation, which is the grave. A hope that ignores his condition is no help to him.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?

events.title: Bildad describes the wicked person’s ruin
events.summary: Bildad speaks again and is offended. He asks why Job treats his friends as stupid animals. He asks whether the earth should be rearranged for Job’s sake. The light of the wicked goes out. His own schemes throw him down, and traps wait on every side. Terrors chase him, and disease eats his skin. His tent is destroyed, and his name is forgotten. He leaves no child or descendant among his people.
events.detail: Verses 8–10 use six different words for traps and snares. Bildad says the wicked man walks into them by his own feet. The speech is framed as a general truth. Its details are not general. Disease consumes the skin (verse 13), and the tent is ruined (verse 15). Verse 19 says he has no child left. Each item matches what happened to Job.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?

events.title: Job asks for pity and a defender
events.summary: Job asks how long his friends will crush him with words. He says God has wronged him and closed his path. God has stripped his honor and uprooted his hope. His relatives, guests, and servants treat him as a stranger. His wife and children turn from him. He begs his friends for pity. He wishes his words were cut in rock forever. He says he knows his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
events.detail: Verses 13–19 list every bond Job has lost, from brothers to servants to wife. The three friends are all he has left. Verse 21 begs them twice for pity. Verse 22 says they pursue him as God does. Since they give none, he turns elsewhere. He wants a written record (verses 23–24) and a living Redeemer (verse 25). In Leviticus 25:25 a redeemer is a relative who steps in to help.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ. A redeemer saves or defends someone. What help does Job hope for?

events.title: Zophar says wicked success ends quickly
events.summary: Zophar says Job’s insult forces him to reply. He says the joy of the wicked is short. A wicked man may rise to the sky, yet he vanishes like a dream. His children must repay the poor. Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to poison inside him. He swallows riches and vomits them up. He crushed the poor and seized houses he did not build. Heaven exposes his guilt, and God’s anger is his portion.
events.detail: Zophar builds his speech on pictures of eating (verses 12–23). Wickedness tastes sweet and then turns to venom. Verse 15 says God makes the man vomit up his wealth. The claim under the pictures is in verse 5. The success of the wicked is brief. Verse 19 adds a charge of crushing the poor, with no proof. This is Zophar’s last speech, and Job answers it with evidence in chapter 21.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?

events.title: Job points to wicked people who prosper
events.summary: Job asks his friends to listen, and that will be their comfort. He asks why the wicked live long and grow strong. Their children are settled, and their houses are safe. They sing and dance and die in peace. They tell God to leave them alone. Job asks how often their lamp really goes out. One person dies at ease and another in bitterness, and both lie in the dust. Travelers report that the evil man is spared and buried with honor.
events.detail: The friends argue from a rule. Job argues in this chapter from what people can see. Verse 7 puts his question plainly. Verse 8 answers Bildad’s claim that the wicked leave no children (18:19). Verse 13 answers Zophar’s claim that their joy is short (20:5). In verse 19 he rejects the idea that the children pay later. Psalm 73:3–12 and Jeremiah 12:1 raise the same question.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering. What does Job ask in verse 7?

events.title: Eliphaz names sins he assumes Job committed
events.summary: Eliphaz speaks a third time. He asks whether God gains anything from a person’s goodness. He says Job’s wickedness must be great. He accuses Job of taking pledges from the poor and stripping them. He says Job refused water, bread, and help to widows and orphans. That is why traps and terror surround him. Job should make peace with God and return to him. Then God will hear his prayers and make his ways bright.
events.detail: Until now the friends have hinted at guilt. In verses 6–9 Eliphaz names crimes. He offers no witness and no instance. The charges are built to fit the theory that suffering proves sin. Chapter 1:8 gives God’s own opposite verdict. Job will answer each charge in 29:12–16 and 31:16–22. Verse 30 says a clean man’s prayer can rescue the guilty (see 42:8).
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help. What does Eliphaz accuse Job of in verse 6?

events.title: Job searches for God’s court
events.summary: Job says his complaint is still bitter. He wishes he knew where to find God. He would lay out his case and hear the answer. He believes God would listen and not overpower him. He looks east, west, north, and south and cannot see God. Yet God knows the way Job takes. When tested, he says, he will come out like gold. Still he is terrified, for God does whatever he chooses.
events.detail: Job wants a courtroom, and he is confident of a fair hearing (verses 6–7). His problem in verse 3 is that he cannot find the judge. Verses 8–9 search in four directions and find no one. Verse 10 turns the matter around. Job cannot see God, but God sees Job’s path. He expects the test to prove him gold. Verses 15–16 show that this trust and his fear exist together.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions. What does Job wish he knew in verse 3?

events.title: Job describes the suffering of the poor
events.summary: Job asks why God does not keep set times for judgment. People move boundary stones and steal flocks. They take the orphan’s donkey and the widow’s ox. The poor go naked in the cold and cling to rocks for shelter. They carry sheaves and go hungry. They tread the winepress and are thirsty. The dying groan in the city, and God charges no one. Murderers, adulterers, and thieves work in the dark.
events.detail: Job’s complaint now reaches past his own house. Verses 2–11 describe the poor in close detail. Workers carry grain while hungry and press grapes while thirsty (verses 10–11). Verse 12 gathers it up: the wounded cry out from the city. Job says God does not treat this as wrong. Eliphaz has just accused Job of crushing such people (22:6–9). This chapter shows whose side Job takes.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses other Church scripture to study suffering. Which examples show Job’s concern for people beyond himself?

events.title: Bildad questions human purity
events.summary: Bildad gives the last and shortest speech of the three friends. He says rule and awe belong to God. God makes peace in his high places. His armies cannot be counted, and his light rises on everyone. Bildad asks how a human can be right before God. Even the moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight. A human being, he says, is a maggot and a worm.
events.detail: The friends’ third round is running out of things to say. Bildad has six verses, and Zophar will not speak at all. Verse 4 repeats what Eliphaz said twice (4:17; 15:14). Job himself granted the point long ago (9:2). It does not touch his question about injustice in chapter 24. Verse 6 calls a human being a worm. In 1:8 God spoke of Job with pride.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?

events.title: Job describes power beyond human knowledge
events.summary: Job answers Bildad with scorn. He asks how Bildad has helped the weak or advised the unwise. Then Job describes God’s power himself. The dead tremble, and the grave lies open before God. He hangs the earth on nothing. He wraps water in clouds and marks the edge of light and dark. By his power the sea is stilled. These are only the fringes of his ways, a faint whisper.
events.detail: Verses 2–4 are sarcasm. Bildad’s speech was grand, and it helped no one. Job then praises God’s power better than Bildad did (verses 5–14). He shows that knowledge of God’s greatness is not what divides them. They all believe it. Verse 14 calls everything he has listed a whisper. Job claims to know less about God than his friends claim.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?

events.title: Job holds to his innocence
events.summary: Job swears an oath by the living God, who has denied him justice. As long as he breathes, he will not speak falsely. He will never say that his friends are right. He will hold to his integrity until he dies. He asks what hope the godless have when God cuts them off. He then describes the fate of the wicked. Their children fall, and their silver passes to others. A storm sweeps them away in the night.
events.detail: The friends offer Job a way out: confess, and be restored. Verse 5 calls that a lie he will not tell. He swears by the same God he says has wronged him (verse 2). Verse 6 says he holds fast his righteousness. God used that very language about him in 2:3. His wife used it against him in 2:9. Verses 13–23 sound like the friends’ view, and readers explain that in different ways.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?

events.title: Where can wisdom be found?
events.summary: This chapter is a poem about wisdom. People mine silver, gold, iron, and copper from the earth. Miners hang on ropes in shafts far from where anyone lives. They find sapphires where no bird or lion has gone. Yet no one knows where wisdom is found. It cannot be bought with gold or jewels. The sea and the grave do not hold it. God alone knows its place, and he says the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
events.detail: Verses 1–11 admire human skill. Miners reach places the falcon and the lion have never seen (verses 7–8). Verse 12 then asks the question that skill cannot answer. Wisdom is not in the deep, and no price buys it (verses 14–19). Verse 28 gives God’s word to humans. To fear the Lord is wisdom, and to turn from evil is understanding. Those are the words used of Job in 1:1.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?

events.title: Job remembers respect and service
events.summary: Job begins his last speech by remembering better days. God’s lamp shone over him, and his children were around him. When he went to the city gate, young men stepped aside and elders stood. Princes stopped talking. He rescued the poor and the orphan. He was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He searched out the case of the stranger. People waited for his words as for rain.
events.detail: Verse 12 begins with “because.” Job’s honor at the gate had a cause. Verses 12–17 list it: the poor, the orphan, the dying, the widow. He was eyes, feet, and a father to people in need. Verse 16 says he looked into the cases of strangers. Eliphaz charged him with wronging these same groups (22:6–9). Job answers with his record, point by point.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?

events.title: Job describes shame and unanswered cries
events.summary: Now, Job says, younger men mock him. Their fathers were outcasts he would not have hired. He has become their song, and they spit at him. God has loosened his bowstring and humbled him. Pain gnaws his bones at night. He cries to God and gets no answer. He once wept for people in trouble, yet evil came when he hoped for good. His harp is tuned to mourning.
events.detail: The word “now” opens three parts of this chapter (verses 1, 9, 16). Each sets the present against the honor of chapter 29. Verse 20 names the deepest loss. Job cries out, and God does not answer. He stands, and God only looks at him. Verse 25 recalls that he wept for others in their hard days. He gave what he does not receive.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?

events.title: Job gives his final defense
events.summary: Job makes his final defense as a series of oaths. If he has lied, lusted, or cheated, let him be punished. He did not reject the complaints of his servants. One God made both him and them in the womb. He shared his bread with orphans and clothed the poor. He did not trust in gold or worship the sun and moon. He did not rejoice at an enemy’s ruin. He signs his defense and asks the Almighty to answer.
events.detail: Job asks for a fair weighing of his life in verse 6. An even balance is an honest scale. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. Verses 13–15 ground a servant’s rights in one Maker of both. His standard reaches inward, to the eyes and to gloating (verses 1 and 29). In verse 35 he signs and demands a reply. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him. What does Job ask for in verse 6?

events.title: Elihu begins after the others fall silent
events.summary: The three friends stop answering, since Job holds that he is right. A younger man named Elihu has been listening. He is angry with Job for justifying himself and not God. He is angry with the friends for condemning Job without an answer. He waited because they were older. Now he says understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from years. He is full of words like wine with no vent. He promises to flatter no one.
