events.detail: Verse 8 states Elihu’s claim to speak. Wisdom comes from the Almighty’s breath, so age does not decide it (verse 9). That is a fair point against the three older men. The chapter also says four times that he was angry (verses 2–5). Verses 18–20 describe a man bursting to talk. Neither Job nor God ever answers Elihu. Chapter 42:7 names the three friends and leaves him out.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?

events.title: Elihu says suffering can teach
events.summary: Elihu asks Job to listen and answer if he can. He is made of clay as Job is, so Job need not fear him. He quotes Job’s claim to be innocent and wronged. He says Job is not right, for God is greater than man. God speaks in dreams to turn people from pride. He also warns through pain on a sickbed. A messenger may plead for the sick person and find a ransom. God does this again and again to bring a soul back from the pit.
events.detail: Job wanted someone on his own level to hear him (9:32–33). In verse 6 Elihu offers himself as that equal. He adds an idea the three friends did not develop. Suffering may warn and teach; it is not only a penalty (verses 16–19). Verses 29–30 say God uses it to bring people back. That is a real advance in the debate. It still assumes Job needed correcting, which 1:8 denies.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?

events.title: Elihu defends God’s justice
events.summary: Elihu speaks to the wise men who are listening. He quotes Job as saying God has taken away his right. He says Job drinks scorn like water and keeps company with evildoers. God cannot do wrong and repays each person’s work. If God withdrew his breath, all flesh would die. He shows no favor to princes over the poor. He sees every step and needs no inquiry. Elihu concludes that Job adds rebellion to his sin.
events.detail: Verse 10 states a principle that the whole Bible affirms. God does not do wickedness. Elihu then uses it as a verdict on Job. If God is just, the man who complains must be wrong. Verse 11 repeats the friends’ rule that God repays each one’s work. Verses 7–8 accuse Job of walking with the wicked and cite nothing. A true principle takes the place of a hearing.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?

events.title: Elihu challenges Job’s complaint
events.summary: Elihu asks whether Job thinks he is more right than God. He tells Job to look at the sky, far above him. Human sin does not harm God, and human goodness gives him nothing. Such things affect only other people. The oppressed cry out under the strong. Yet no one asks for God their Maker, who gives songs in the night. God does not answer an empty cry. So Job, who says he cannot see God, must wait.
events.detail: Elihu grants in verse 9 that the oppressed cry out. Job said the same in 24:12. Elihu then explains why no answer comes. They cry from pain and do not truly seek God (verse 10). Verse 12 blames their pride. So an unanswered prayer becomes the fault of the one who prays. Job has already said his own prayer is pure (16:17).
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?

events.title: Elihu describes correction and the storm
events.summary: Elihu says he has more to say on God’s behalf. God is mighty and despises no one. He does not keep the wicked alive, and he gives the afflicted their rights. When people are bound in suffering, he shows them their wrong. If they listen, they finish their days in good. If not, they die without knowledge. Elihu warns Job not to turn toward evil. He then praises God, who draws up water and sends rain and thunder.
events.detail: Verse 15 sums up Elihu’s best thought. God rescues the afflicted by means of their affliction. Pain can open a person’s ear. Verses 11–12 then attach the old bargain: obey and prosper, refuse and perish. Job obeyed, and he did not prosper. So the teaching and a threat share one speech. In verses 27–33 Elihu turns to the storm, which prepares for chapter 38.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?

events.title: Elihu asks Job to consider God’s works
events.summary: Elihu’s heart pounds at the thunder. He says God’s voice roars, and lightning reaches the ends of the earth. God tells the snow and the rain to fall. Animals take cover, and ice forms by God’s breath. Clouds turn wherever he guides them. Elihu tells Job to stand still and consider these works. He asks whether Job knows how clouds are balanced. He ends by saying the Almighty is beyond reach and does not oppress.
events.detail: Verse 14 asks Job to stop and look at God’s works. Elihu’s questions in verses 15–18 sound like the ones God will ask. Verse 13 allows a storm more than one purpose. It may come for correction, for the land, or for kindness. That is wider than the friends’ single rule. A real storm seems to be gathering as he speaks. In 38:1 the LORD answers from the whirlwind.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?

events.title: The Lord answers from the whirlwind
events.summary: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. He asks who darkens counsel with words without knowledge. He asks where Job was when the earth’s foundations were laid. The morning stars sang then, and the sons of God shouted for joy. He asks who shut in the sea and commanded the dawn. He asks about the gates of death and the storehouses of snow. He sends rain on deserts where no one lives. He asks who feeds the lion and the raven.
events.detail: Job asked for a hearing and thought none would come (23:3; 30:20). In verse 1 the LORD comes and speaks to him. The answer does not explain Job’s suffering. It never mentions the accuser or any charge. Verse 4 begins a long series of questions about the making of the world. Verses 26–27 describe rain falling where no person lives. The world is not arranged around human use or human reward.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth. What does God ask Job about creation?

events.title: The Lord describes wild animals
events.summary: The LORD continues to question Job about wild animals. He asks whether Job knows when mountain goats give birth. He asks who set the wild donkey free to roam the salt land. The wild ox will not plow or stay in a barn. The ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground and laughs at horse and rider. The war horse charges into battle without fear. The hawk flies south, and the eagle nests on the high cliff.
events.detail: Every animal in this chapter lives outside human control. Verse 5 asks who set the wild donkey free. Verses 7–8 show it scorning the city and ranging the hills. The wild ox serves no farmer (verses 9–12). The ostrich lacks sense, and God made her so (verses 13–17). The friends described a tidy world. God shows one full of misfits.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view. Who set the wild donkey free (verse 5)?

events.title: Job falls silent and hears about behemoth
events.summary: The LORD asks whether the one who argues with the Almighty will correct him. Job answers that he is small and will say no more. The LORD speaks again from the whirlwind. He asks whether Job will condemn him in order to be right. He asks whether Job has an arm like God’s. Let Job humble every proud person and crush the wicked. Then God will admit that Job can save himself. He points to Behemoth, a huge creature that he made.
events.detail: Verse 8 names the real issue between them. To be in the right, Job has put God in the wrong. The friends did the reverse and put Job in the wrong. Both sides assumed that one of the two must be condemned. Verses 10–14 hand Job the task of governing. Let him bring down every proud person in the world. Running justice turns out to be harder than demanding it.
events.uncertainty: The point shows the Jordan, which the poem names. It does not show Job’s home.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views. What does God ask Job in verse 8?

events.title: The Lord describes Leviathan
events.summary: The LORD describes Leviathan, a creature of the deep. No one can catch him with a hook or make him a servant. No one will play with him like a bird or sell him in the market. Harpoons and spears are useless. His scales are like rows of sealed shields. Fire and smoke come from his mouth. Iron is like straw to him. He looks down on everything proud and is king over them.
events.detail: Verses 1–7 ask whether Job can hook, bind, bargain with, or sell this creature. Verse 8 warns him to try once and remember it. Verse 10 draws the point. If no one dares to rouse Leviathan, who can stand before its maker? Verse 11 adds that God owes nothing to anyone. That answers the accuser’s question about serving God for pay (1:9). It also answers the friends’ view of reward as wages.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?

events.title: Job answers and prays for his friends
events.summary: Job answers the LORD. He says God can do all things. He admits that he spoke of things too wonderful for him. He had heard of God, and now his eye sees him. The LORD tells Eliphaz that the three friends did not speak rightly, as Job did. They must bring offerings, and Job will pray for them. When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes. Job receives twice as much, ten more children, and a long life.
events.detail: Verse 7 changes how every speech in the book should be read. God says the friends did not speak rightly about him. He says his servant Job did, and repeats it in verse 8. Job protested, and the friends defended God. The honest protest is judged truer than the false defense. The friends now need the prayer of the man they accused. Verse 10 ties Job’s restoration to that prayer.
events.uncertainty: Job lives in the land of Uz. No one knows for sure where Uz was.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s renewed life with hope after loss. What must the friends do after God corrects them?

guides.title: Job: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: The reader knows what the friends do not
steps.text: The book’s first verse gives a verdict before any trouble comes. Job is blameless and upright, fears God, and turns from evil. The LORD repeats those words in verse 8. Satan’s question in verse 9 sets the test: is such goodness only paid for? Job and his friends never hear this scene in heaven. The reader does. Every later claim that Job must have sinned is already known to be wrong.

steps.title: A measure becomes an image of justice
steps.text: Job asks for a fair weighing of his life in verse 6. An even balance is an honest scale. He then names concrete duties toward workers, poor people, and strangers. Verses 13–15 ground a servant’s rights in one Maker of both. His standard reaches inward, to the eyes and to gloating (verses 1 and 29). In verse 35 he signs and demands a reply. An ancient trade weight helps explain the image without identifying Job’s time or home.

steps.title: The final judgment changes how the speeches should be read
steps.text: Verse 7 changes how every speech in the book should be read. God says the friends did not speak rightly about him. He says his servant Job did, and repeats it in verse 8. Job protested, and the friends defended God. The honest protest is judged truer than the false defense. The friends now need the prayer of the man they accused. Verse 10 ties Job’s restoration to that prayer.

chapterMaps.narrative: Job lives in the land of Uz and is blameless and rich. He has seven sons and three daughters and offers sacrifices for them. In heaven the accuser, called Satan, comes before the LORD. The LORD praises Job, and Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing. The LORD lets him take all that Job has. In one day raiders, fire, and a great wind destroy his herds, servants, and children. Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships. He says the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away.

chapterMaps.narrative: Satan comes before the LORD again. He says a man will give anything to save his own skin. The LORD lets him strike Job’s body but spare his life. Job is covered with painful sores from head to foot. He sits in ashes and scrapes himself with broken pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that people must accept hardship from God as well as good. Three friends come to comfort him and sit with him in silence for a week.

chapterMaps.narrative: After seven days Job speaks. He curses the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He wants that day turned to darkness and left out of the calendar. He asks why he did not die at birth. In the grave, he says, the weary rest and the slave is free. He asks why life is given to people in misery. What he feared most has happened. He has no ease, no quiet, and no rest.

Eliphaz asks who ever perished while innocent. In his experience those who sow trouble reap it. He tells of a night vision that made his bones shake. A voice asked whether a mortal can be more just than God. Even God’s servants in heaven are not beyond fault.

In Job’s place he would take his case to God. God does great things, sends rain, and lifts up the lowly. The person God corrects is happy, so Job should not reject discipline. God wounds, and he also heals. Job will yet have safety, many children, and a long life.

He asks them to show him plainly where he has gone wrong.

He asks why God watches a human being so closely. He asks why God does not pardon him before he lies in the dust.

chapterMaps.narrative: Job begins his last speech by remembering better days. God’s lamp shone over him, and his children were around him. When he went to the city gate, young men stepped aside and elders stood. Princes stopped talking. He rescued the poor and the orphan. He was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He searched out the case of the stranger. People waited for his words as for rain.

chapterMaps.narrative: Now, Job says, younger men mock him. Their fathers were outcasts he would not have hired. He has become their song, and they spit at him. God has loosened his bowstring and humbled him. Pain gnaws his bones at night. He cries to God and gets no answer. He once wept for people in trouble, yet evil came when he hoped for good. His harp is tuned to mourning.

chapterMaps.narrative: Job makes his final defense as a series of oaths. If he has lied, lusted, or cheated, let him be punished. He did not reject the complaints of his servants. One God made both him and them in the womb. He shared his bread with orphans and clothed the poor. He did not trust in gold or worship the sun and moon. He did not rejoice at an enemy’s ruin. He signs his defense and asks the Almighty to answer.

chapterMaps.narrative: The three friends stop answering, since Job holds that he is right. A younger man named Elihu has been listening. He is angry with Job for justifying himself and not God. He is angry with the friends for condemning Job without an answer. He waited because they were older. Now he says understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from years. He is full of words like wine with no vent. He promises to flatter no one.

chapterMaps.narrative: Elihu asks Job to listen and answer if he can. He is made of clay as Job is, so Job need not fear him. He quotes Job’s claim to be innocent and wronged. He says Job is not right, for God is greater than man. God speaks in dreams to turn people from pride. He also warns through pain on a sickbed. A messenger may plead for the sick person and find a ransom. God does this again and again to bring a soul back from the pit.

chapterMaps.narrative: Elihu speaks to the wise men who are listening. He quotes Job as saying God has taken away his right. He says Job drinks scorn like water and keeps company with evildoers. God cannot do wrong and repays each person’s work. If God withdrew his breath, all flesh would die. He shows no favor to princes over the poor. He sees every step and needs no inquiry. Elihu concludes that Job adds rebellion to his sin.

chapterMaps.narrative: Elihu asks whether Job thinks he is more right than God. He tells Job to look at the sky, far above him. Human sin does not harm God, and human goodness gives him nothing. Such things affect only other people. The oppressed cry out under the strong. Yet no one asks for God their Maker, who gives songs in the night. God does not answer an empty cry. So Job, who says he cannot see God, must wait.

chapterMaps.narrative: Elihu says he has more to say on God’s behalf. God is mighty and despises no one. He does not keep the wicked alive, and he gives the afflicted their rights. When people are bound in suffering, he shows them their wrong. If they listen, they finish their days in good. If not, they die without knowledge. Elihu warns Job not to turn toward evil. He then praises God, who draws up water and sends rain and thunder.

chapterMaps.narrative: Elihu’s heart pounds at the thunder. He says God’s voice roars, and lightning reaches the ends of the earth. God tells the snow and the rain to fall. Animals take cover, and ice forms by God’s breath. Clouds turn wherever he guides them. Elihu tells Job to stand still and consider these works. He asks whether Job knows how clouds are balanced. He ends by saying the Almighty is beyond reach and does not oppress.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. He asks who darkens counsel with words without knowledge. He asks where Job was when the earth’s foundations were laid. The morning stars sang then, and the sons of God shouted for joy. He asks who shut in the sea and commanded the dawn. He asks about the gates of death and the storehouses of snow. He sends rain on deserts where no one lives. He asks who feeds the lion and the raven.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD continues to question Job about wild animals. He asks whether Job knows when mountain goats give birth. He asks who set the wild donkey free to roam the salt land. The wild ox will not plow or stay in a barn. The ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground and laughs at horse and rider. The war horse charges into battle without fear. The hawk flies south, and the eagle nests on the high cliff.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD asks whether the one who argues with the Almighty will correct him. Job answers that he is small and will say no more. The LORD speaks again from the whirlwind. He asks whether Job will condemn him in order to be right. He asks whether Job has an arm like God’s. Let Job humble every proud person and crush the wicked. Then God will admit that Job can save himself. He points to Behemoth, a huge creature that he made.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD describes Leviathan, a creature of the deep. No one can catch him with a hook or make him a servant. No one will play with him like a bird or sell him in the market. Harpoons and spears are useless. His scales are like rows of sealed shields. Fire and smoke come from his mouth. Iron is like straw to him. He looks down on everything proud and is king over them.

chapterMaps.narrative: Job answers the LORD. He says God can do all things. He admits that he spoke of things too wonderful for him. He had heard of God, and now his eye sees him. The LORD tells Eliphaz that the three friends did not speak rightly, as Job did. They must bring offerings, and Job will pray for them. When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes. Job receives twice as much, ten more children, and a long life.
